program_plain: World: a 64x64 lattice of cells (wrap-around edges, 8 neighbours each). Cells have 3 types (type 0 = empty, 10% of cells; random start). Rules each step: an occupied cell whose same-type share among occupied neighbours is below 0.3 moves to a random empty cell.
model_family: Schelling segregation model (lattice agent-based / statistical physics of social dynamics; Kawasaki-like vacancy exchange)
citations: Schelling 1971, J. Math. Sociol. 1:143-186 - original dynamic segregation models; mild same-type preference -> clustering

Dall'Asta, Castellano & Marsili 2008, J. Stat. Mech. L07002 (arXiv 0707.1681) - statistical physics of Schelling; unhappy agents jump to random vacancies; stationary regime with constant unhappy density
Gauvin, Vannimenus & Nadal 2009, Eur. Phys. J. B 70:293 (arXiv 0903.4694) - phase diagram vs tolerance and vacancy density; mixed-to-segregated transitions
Vinkovic & Kirman 2006, PNAS 103(51):19261-19265 - physical analogue; clustering driven by surface tension
Fossett 2008, PNAS 105:4109 - Schelling-type simulations with more than two groups
Castellano, Fortunato & Loreto 2009, Rev. Mod. Phys. 81:591 - review (seen only in reference list of arXiv 1705.08586)
searches: Schelling 1971 Dynamic models of segregation Journal of Mathematical Sociology
Schelling segregation model multiple types tolerance threshold random relocation to vacant sites review physics
Vinkovic Kirman 2006 A physical analogue of the Schelling model PNAS
Schelling model more than two groups three types segregation threshold simulation Moore neighborhood
notes: The 'rising activity' trend and the exact sign convention of g_moran=-1.5 were not matched to a specific source. Three types with threshold 0.3 sits near the random-mixing like-share (~1/3), so weak/slow segregation and persistent churn are expected. Unconditional random relocation means there is no absorbing frozen state.
full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** This is the Schelling segregation model, in the random-relocation variant with three groups. The "activity rising" feature is the one part I could not match to a specific source.

**1. Model family.** The rules are a lattice agent-based model from opinion/social dynamics and statistical physics. Occupied cells are agents on a torus with vacancies and a Moore (8-cell) neighbourhood. An agent is unhappy if its like-type share among occupied neighbours is below a threshold, and unhappy agents jump to a random vacancy. This is Schelling's model.

**2. Earliest source and the behaviour.**
- Schelling (1969, *American Economic Review* 59, 488) and, in more detail, Schelling, "Dynamic models of segregation", J. Math. Sociol. 1, 143–186 (1971). The 1971 abstract describes a simulation in which members of two recognizable groups distribute themselves in neighborhoods defined by reference to their own locations. Its central finding is that mild same-type preferences produce large-scale clustering.
- The closest match to your exact rule is the physics literature. In Dall'Asta, Castellano & Marsili's work (arXiv 0707.1681, "Statistical physics of the Schelling model of segregation", J. Stat. Mech. 2008, L07002), only unhappy agents move, and they move to vacancies at any distance. In their unconstrained version, the system can enter a stationary regime in which the density of unhappy individuals stays constant on average.
- Your rule is also described in popular write-ups. Every agent below the satisfaction threshold relocates at random into a vacant location. In that version, for sufficiently low tolerance and/or vacancy rate no static equilibrium exists, because some individual is always unsatisfied and cannot find another suitable spot. This probably explains your persistently high activity.
- Gauvin, Vannimenus & Nadal, "Phase diagram of a Schelling segregation model" (Eur. Phys. J. B 70, 293, 2009; arXiv 0903.4694). They report an abrupt change at a threshold T_f from a mixed configuration to one with only two clusters. This is a phase-transition view of the same model.
- Multi-group versions are also published. Fossett (PNAS 105, 4109, 2008; the "Understanding the social context…" paper) moves beyond the Schelling two-colour model to explore segregation patterns in multiple-group settings. It uses three colours.
- Vinković & Kirman (PNAS 103, 19261, 2006) give a physical analogue in which cluster dynamics is driven by a "surface tension" force. This is the physical interpretation of the clustering.

**Review.** Castellano, Fortunato & Loreto, "Statistical physics of social dynamics" (Rev. Mod. Phys. 81, 591, 2009) is the standard review. I saw it only in a reference list (arXiv 1705.08586), not as a source I read. Another review-like source is Gauvin et al.'s 2009 paper above.

**Differences from your system.**
- **Three types instead of two.** This likely matters only quantitatively. A random mix gives a like-share near 1/3, so a threshold of 0.3 sits near the random-mixing level. Segregation should therefore be weak or slow, and many agents stay unhappy. The 0.3 and 0.4 variants should differ mainly in how many agents are unhappy at any time.
- **Movers go to any random vacancy without checking they will be happy there.** This keeps the system from freezing, as the Dall'Asta et al. unconstrained-dynamics result and the no-static-equilibrium remark suggest.
- **"Activity rising".** I found no source reporting this exact trend. It is plausible, because early random mixing is perturbed by moves and clusters form slowly. Treat it as unverified.
- **Moran sign.** Your g_moran of −1.5 is described as "clustering". I could not check how your metric is signed. Clustering is the expected outcome in this model, but I did not confirm the sign convention.

**Confidence: medium-high.** The model identity and its clustering behaviour are well established across several sources I confirmed through the search. Confidence is not higher because I did not find a paper that simulates this exact parameter set (3 types, 10% vacancy, threshold 0.3 or 0.4, unconditional random relocation). I also found no source on the rising-activity trend.

**Searches run.**
- Schelling 1971 Dynamic models of segregation
- Schelling multiple types tolerance threshold random relocation review physics
- Vinković Kirman 2006 physical analogue
- Schelling more than two groups three types Moore neighborhood
